content: Accuracy refers to the degree to which a measured or calculated value conforms to the true or actual value. Precision, on the other hand, refers to the consistency or reproducibility of measurements, indicating how closely repeated measurements or calculations agree with each other. A result can be accurate but not precise, precise but not accurate, neither, or both. A result is considered valid only when it is both accurate and precise. In the context of research, the terms error and bias are often used. Error refers to random variability, while bias refers to systematic deviations caused by factors unrelated to the independent variable. To illustrate the difference between accuracy and precision, the analogy of a target is often used. Accuracy is represented by how close arrows land to the bullseye, while precision is represented by how tightly grouped the arrows are, regardless of their proximity to the bullseye. For example, if a measuring rod is supposed to be 10 yards long but is actually 9 yards and 35 inches, it may provide consistent (precise) measurements, but those measurements will be consistently incorrect (inaccurate). Achieving accuracy without precision is unreliable because measurements that are not grouped closely cannot all be close to the true value. In logic-level modeling and integrated circuit (IC) simulation, a common mistake is comparing a logic simulation model to a transistor circuit simulation model. This comparison reflects differences in precision, not accuracy. Precision is about the level of detail, while accuracy is about how closely the model reflects reality. Quantifying accuracy and precision involves repeated measurements against a traceable reference standard, such as those defined by the International System of Units (SI) and maintained by organizations like the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Precision is often expressed in terms of standard deviation, while accuracy involves the difference between the mean of measurements and the reference value (bias). Calibration requires identifying and correcting for bias. The combined effect of bias and precision determines overall accuracy. In scientific and engineering contexts, accuracy and precision are often implied through significant figures. However, relying solely on this convention can lead to errors, especially when data sources do not adhere to it. For example, a value of 8.0 implies a higher level of precision than 8 because the first decimal place was measured and found to be zero. Precision can be further categorized into repeatability and reproducibility. Repeatability refers to variation under consistent conditions (same instrument, operator, and short time frame), while reproducibility refers to variation across different instruments, operators, and time periods. A common statistical method for measuring precision is the Six Sigma tool ANOVA Gage R&R. In biostatistics, accuracy is used to describe how well a binary classification test correctly identifies or excludes a condition. It is the proportion of true results (true positives and true negatives) in the population. An accuracy of 100% means the test correctly identifies all individuals as either sick or well. Accuracy can be calculated using sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence. In psychometrics, accuracy and precision are analogous to validity and reliability, respectively. Validity refers to how well a measurement instrument or psychological test measures what it is intended to measure, often established through experiments or correlations with behavior. Reliability refers to the consistency of the measurement, often assessed using statistical techniques like Cronbach's alpha.
